newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia says status of kidnapped Briton unknown.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia says status of kidnapped Briton unknown.

text.p: Cambodia said on Friday it has received no fresh information on the fate of kidnapped Briton Christopher Howes for over three weeks and could no longer offer assurances the mine-clearance expert was still alive.

Nearly a month after announcing that Howes and his Cambodian interpreter, Houn Hourth, had escaped from Khmer Rouge captivity, government officials said they had no information on the fate of the two men.
"There is no information to confirm they are alive," co-Minister of Defence Tea Banh told Reuters. "This has become a very complicated problem."
Howes and Houn Hourth were abducted by armed men on March 26 in the northwest province of Siem Reap while conducting mine clearance activities for the British Mines Advisory Group.

On November 21, deputy chief of staff Lieutenant-General Nhiek Bun Chhay said the two men had escaped from the hardline guerrilla base of Anlong Veng near the Thai border with the help of Khmer Rouge defectors.
At the time, Nhiek Bun Chhay said he was told through a Khmer Rouge go-between that the men were healthy but thin, and thought they would arrive in Phnom Penh soon.
But the men failed to show up, and three separate attempts to meet the hostages at different locations were unsuccessful.
Nhiek Bun Chhay has since said he has no further information on the case.

"According to the first reports, they were helped by a group of Khmer Rouge defectors to escape from captivity and were still alive, but there was a conflict between the helpers and the Khmer Rouge along the way," said Tea Banh.
Government officials had reported sounds of fighting near the third and last pre-arranged meeting place with the hostages, but the reports were unconfirmed.
After their abduction in March, the two men were forced to make land mines for the Khmer Rouge, government officials have said.
But in a response to a request for information from King Norodom Sihanouk, Khmer Rouge nominal leader Khieu Samphan has denied that his hardline troops were involved in the kidnapping.
The Khmer Rouge, who ruled the country by terror during Pol Pot's 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime, has been fighting the coalition government that emerged after U.N.-run general elections in 1993.
The guerrilla movement has been badly hit by massive defections in recent months, and only about 800 to 2,000 hardliners are thought to remain in Anlong Veng.
